present_on_scene_date.note: THE RECORD PLACES THIS PERSON NOWHERE ON THE DAY, BECAUSE HE WAS DEAD. The old settlers' obituary dates the death 25 October 1830, before the scene date of 1 July 1835, and no record that places a person at Chicago names this one after it. A DEATH NOTICE IS NOT A PRESENCE (T-1131): the old settlers' obituary declares `places_in_1835: false` on every record it publishes, because its own header admits it prints citizens who arrived after 1843. It dates a death; it never says the man was standing in the town on 1 July 1835 — so it cannot be the at-or-before leg of a bracket, and a later source on the far side cannot close one over a dead man. `absent` and not `uncertain`: a silence is somewhere the sources have not looked, and a death is not a silence.

OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — CORROBORATION, NOT A NEW FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's fourth annual reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, held 18 May 1882, printed this man among the guests present as “Wolcott, Alexander, City-Hall, Chicago.” (Chicago Tribune, 19 May 1882). The club's criterion was residence in Chicago before 1 January 1840 and majority by then: the roster therefore corroborates a pre-1840 Chicago residence and says he was alive in 1882. It gives NO year of arrival, and the address it prints is where he lived in 1882, forty-seven years after the scene date — it is not an 1835 residence and is not read as one. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Wolcott, Alexander, | 1834, June 4, | Middletown, Conn. | 64 | Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. AND THIS CARD CONTRADICTS ITSELF ON THE POINT: it already carries a death notice, “Wolcott, Dr. Alexander”, dated Oct. 25, 1830 — before the register was signed. A man dead by then did not sign it, so either the register's entry is another man of the same name or this card is two men. Nothing is withdrawn and no record is split here; the case is filed in data/research/old_settlers/receptions.json under os_q_registered_after_a_documented_death for the identity master (T-0513). Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 10 times, as “WOLCOTT ALEXANDER”, 1830-09-27 to 1830-09-29: 2 federal land entries — E2NE sec 09 T39N R14E; E2NEVO sec 09 T39N R14E and 8 lots in the platted town — lot 1 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L1BL1CHIOT, as printed); lot 2 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L2BL1CHIOT, as printed); lot 3 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L3BL1CHIOT, as printed); lot 4 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L4BL1CHIOT, as printed); lot 5 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L5BL1CHIOT, as printed); lot 6 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L6BL1CHIOT, as printed); lot 7 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L7BL1CHIOT, as printed); lot 8 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L8BL1CHIOT, as printed), 160.00 acres stated in all, for $945.00 (ls0055, ls0056, ls1550, ls1551, ls1552, ls1553, ls1554, ls1555, ls1556, ls1557). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS ILLINOIS, UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $685.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: WOLCOTT ALEXANDER matches Alexander Wolcott: the forename names Alexander Wolcott of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Wolcott, Alexander” (tax_1833_110, line 162). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. old_settler_deaths.note: LATER EVIDENCE OF A DEATH, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. Fergus's 1843 directory (1896) prints an obituary list of old settlers, and one of its entries meets somebody of this name. THE HEADER OF THE LIST IS QUOTED ABOVE, and it is the limit the whole reading turns on. It does not mean the person was in Chicago in 1835, and it does not mean they arrived before 1843 — the list's own header, quoted above, says it also names citizens who arrived later and others merely 'prominently connected with Illinois history'. A match means one thing: a name in the 1835 layer and a name in this list agree on surname and first initial, and the list gives that name a death date and an age. The date and the interval are the payload. Whatever is carried is carried as evidence of a DEATH and of an interval the birth falls in, never as an 1835 fact and never as a grade. T-0513 consolidates and T-0514/T-0515 apply; this file changes no record. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. A death notice printed in 1896 says a person of this name died on a day; under the ratified ladder (T-0513) that is later evidence about a DEATH, and it is never an 1835 residence. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.
